claim: MEG activity was measured as participants read highly constraining sentences in which the final words could be predicted.
source: MEG activity was measured as participants read highly constraining sentences in which the final words could be predicted.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the experimental procedure.

claim: Before the onset of the predicted words, both the spatial and temporal patterns of brain activity were more similar when the same words were predicted than when different words were predicted.
source: Before the onset of the predicted words, both the spatial and temporal patterns of brain activity were more similar when the same words were predicted than when different words were predicted.
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract, supported by MEG data analysis.

claim: The temporal patterns localized to the left inferior and medial temporal lobe.
source: The temporal patterns localized to the left inferior and medial temporal lobe.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a result of source localization analysis.

claim: Unique spatial and temporal patterns of neural activity are associated with item-specific lexico-semantic predictions.
source: These findings provide evidence that unique spatial and temporal patterns of neural activity are associated with item-specific lexico-semantic predictions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: The unique spatial patterns reflected the prediction of spatially distributed semantic features associated with the predicted word.
source: We suggest that the unique spatial patterns reflected the prediction of spatially distributed semantic features associated with the predicted word, and that the left inferior/medial temporal lobe played a role in temporally 'binding' these features, giving rise to unique lexico-semantic predictions.
evidence: This is an interpretation proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: The left inferior/medial temporal lobe played a role in temporally 'binding' semantic features, giving rise to unique lexico-semantic predictions.
source: We suggest that the unique spatial patterns reflected the prediction of spatially distributed semantic features associated with the predicted word, and that the left inferior/medial temporal lobe played a role in temporally 'binding' these features, giving rise to unique lexico-semantic predictions.
evidence: This is an interpretation proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Prediction is hypothesized to be a core computational principle of brain function.
source: Prediction is hypothesized to be a core computational principle of brain function (Clark, 2013; Mumford, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: During language processing, probabilistic prediction at multiple levels of representation allows us to rapidly understand what we read or hear by giving processing a head start.
source: During language processing, probabilistic prediction at multiple levels of representation allows us to rapidly understand what we read or hear by giving processing a head start (see Kuperberg and Jaeger, 2016a, for a review).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In highly constraining sentence contexts, we are able to predict the semantic features of upcoming words.
source: However, there is now clear neural evidence that, at least in highly constraining sentence contexts, we are able to predict the semantic features of upcoming words.
evidence: This is stated as established neural evidence in the field.

claim: The N400 is an event related potential (ERP) that reflects semantic processing.
source: First, a large body of studies show that the N400 — an event related potential (ERP) that reflects semantic processing — is reduced in response to words whose semantic features match semantic predictions generated by highly predictable (versus less predictable) contexts.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of cognitive neuroscience.

claim: The N400 is reduced in response to words whose semantic features match semantic predictions generated by highly predictable contexts.
source: First, a large body of studies show that the N400 — an event related potential (ERP) that reflects semantic processing — is reduced in response to words whose semantic features match semantic predictions generated by highly predictable (versus less predictable) contexts. For example, the N400 elicited by 'baby' is smaller in the constraining context 'In the crib, there is a sleeping …' than in the less constraining context, 'Under the tree, there is a sleeping …' (Federmeier and Kutas, 1999; Kutas and Federmeier, 2011; Kuperberg, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Several studies have reported differential modulation of brain activity following highly predictable versus less predictable sentence contexts, prior to the onset of predicted words.
source: Second, several studies have reported differential modulation of brain activity following highly predictable versus less predictable sentence contexts, prior to the onset of predicted words. These include larger negative-going ERP effects (Freunberger and Roehm, 2017; Grisoni et al., 2017; León-Cabrera et al., 2017; Maess et al., 2016), increases in theta power (Dikker and Pylkkänen, 2013; Piai et al., 2016), and the suppression of alpha/beta power (Piai et al., 2014; Piai et al., 2015; Rommers et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Anticipatory effects have been neuroanatomically localized to both neocortical and subcortical regions.
source: These anticipatory effects have been neuroanatomically localized to both neocortical (e.g. left frontal and temporal regions; Dikker and Pylkkänen, 2013; Piai et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018) and subcortical (e.g. hippocampus and cerebellum; Bonhage et al., 2015; Lesage et al., 2017; Piai et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018) regions.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies have averaged across items that predict different upcoming words, leaving unclear whether the brain produces unique patterns of neural activity that correspond to the prediction of item-specific lexico-semantic representations.
source: Importantly, however, previous studies have averaged across items that predict different upcoming words. It therefore remains unclear whether the brain produces unique patterns of neural activity that correspond to the prediction of item-specific lexico-semantic representations.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Multivariate Pattern Analysis (MVPA) provides a way of addressing whether the brain produces unique patterns of neural activity for item-specific predictions.
source: Multivariate Pattern Analysis (MVPA) provides one way of addressing this question (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Staudigl et al., 2015; Stokes et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: Correlational approaches were first applied to fMRI data to identify spatial patterns of brain activity representing objects categories in the ventral stream.
source: Correlational approaches were first applied to fMRI data to identify spatial patterns of brain activity representing objects categories in the ventral stream (Haxby et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a seminal study.

claim: The basic assumption of RSA is that similarities in patterns of brain activity reflect similarities between representationally similar items.
source: The basic assumption of RSA is that similarities in patterns of brain activity reflect similarities between representationally similar items.
evidence: This describes the fundamental principle of the RSA method.

claim: Spatial RSA has been used to identify unique patterns of spatial activity during perception, cognition and action.
source: Spatial RSA has been used to identify unique patterns of spatial activity during perception, cognition and action (Kriegeskorte et al., 2007; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RSA has been applied to MEG and EEG data to determine when spatially-specific patterns of neural activity are activated in relation to the appearance of bottom-up input.
source: More recently, it has been applied to MEG and EEG data whose excellent temporal resolution can tell us exactly when such spatially-specific patterns of neural activity are activated in relation to the appearance of bottom-up input (Stokes et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Both spatial and temporal RSA approaches have been successfully used in combination with MEG and EEG to decode representationally specific visual information during perception and working memory maintenance.
source: Both spatial and temporal RSA approaches have been successfully used in combination with MEG and EEG to decode representationally specific visual information during the perception of bottom-up input (Cichy et al., 2014), as well as during its maintenance in working memory in the absence of bottom-up input (Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Participants read 240 sentences with highly constraining contexts that predicted a specific word.
source: Participants read 240 sentences, all with highly constraining contexts that predicted a specific word (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Sentences were visually presented at a slow rate of 1000 ms per word.
source: The sentences were visually presented at a slow rate of 1000 ms per word.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The slow presentation rate ensured the generation of specific lexico-semantic predictions and guaranteed sufficient time to detect any representationally specific neural activity before the onset of the predicted word.
source: This ensured the generation of specific lexico-semantic predictions and guaranteed sufficient time to detect any representationally specific neural activity before the onset of the predicted word.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the experimental design choice.

claim: Sentences were constructed in pairs (120 pairs) such that each member of a pair predicted the same word, even though their contexts differed.
source: We constructed these sentences in pairs (120 pairs) such that each member of a pair predicted the same word, even though their contexts differed (e.g. 'In the crib, there is a sleeping …' and 'In the hospital, there is a newborn …').
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: During the experiment, members of each sentence pair were separated by at least 30 other sentences (on average 88 sentences).
source: During the experiment, sentences were presented in a pseudorandom order, with at least 30 other sentences (on average 88 sentences) in between each member of a given pair.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The multimodal semantic properties and features associated with words are thought to be represented within regions that are spatially distributed across the cortex.
source: There is some evidence that the various semantic features and properties associated with words and concepts are represented in the brain across spatially distributed multimodal networks (Damasio, 1989; Price, 2000; Martin and Chao, 2001), which can be detected using spatial RSA (e.g. Devereux et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Twenty-six participants read 240 sentences while MEG data were acquired.
source: Twenty-six participants read 240 sentences, presented at a rate of one word per second, while MEG data were acquired.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: One member of each sentence pair ended with the predicted word while the other member ended with an unpredicted but plausible word.
source: To avoid repetition of the predicted word across sentence pairs, one member of each pair ended with the predicted word (e.g. in S1, 'baby') while the other member ended with an unpredicted but plausible word (e.g. in S2, 'child').
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Comprehension accuracy was high (98% ± 2.0%).
source: Comprehension accuracy was high (98% ± 2.0%).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: Both the within- and between-pair group-averaged time series of spatial correlation values showed a sharp increase at ~100 ms after the onset of the penultimate word (SFW-1) that lasted ~400 ms before sharply decreasing again.
source: Both the within- and between-pair group-averaged time series of spatial correlation values showed a sharp increase at ~100 ms after the onset of the penultimate word (SFW-1; at −1000 ms) that lasted ~400 ms before sharply decreasing again (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the spatial RSA analysis, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The general increase in spatial similarity is attributed to the visual onset and offset of each word.
source: We attribute this general increase in spatial similarity to the visual onset and offset of each word.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed pattern in the data.

claim: Between −880 and −485 ms before the onset of the SFW, the spatial similarity was greater when the same word was predicted than when different words were predicted (within-pairs >between-pairs: t(25) = 3.751, p < 0.001).
source: Between −880 and −485 ms before the onset of the final word, the spatial similarity was greater when the same word was predicted than when different words were predicted (within-pairs >between-pairs: t(25) = 3.751, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a key statistical result from the spatial RSA analysis, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In most participants (18/26) the within-pair spatial correlations were greater than the between-pair spatial correlations.
source: Eighteen out of 26 subjects had R-values below the diagonal, that is larger values for the within-pair than the between-pair spatial correlations.
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no difference between the within-pair and between-pair spatial correlation values averaged across the −897 – −507 ms interval before the SFW-1.
source: In contrast, there was no difference between the within-pair (R = 0.066 + /- 0.02) and between-pair (R = 0.068 + /- 0.02) spatial correlation values averaged across the −897 – −507 ms interval before the SFW-1 (corresponding to 103–493 ms after the onset of SFW-2): t(25) = −0.937, p = 0.358.
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no effect at an earlier time window.

claim: The difference in spatial similarity prior to the SFW cannot be explained by differences in the number of within-pair and between-pair sentences used to compute mean spatial correlation values.
source: This difference in spatial similarity prior to the SFW cannot be explained by differences in the number of within-pair and between-pair sentences used to compute these mean spatial correlation values. This is because the number of trials per condition can affect the variance of the estimated mean value, but not the value of the estimated mean itself.
evidence: This is a methodological argument based on statistical principles.

claim: The within-pair spatial correlation values remained significantly greater than the between-pair correlations when using a randomly selected subset of between-pair correlations that matched the number of within-pair correlations (t(25) = 2.393, p = 0.025).
source: Nonetheless, to convince skeptics, we repeated the analysis using a randomly selected subset of between-pair correlations that matched the number of within-pair correlations. This analysis confirmed that the within-pair spatial correlation values remained significantly greater than the between-pair correlations (t(25) = 2.393, p = 0.025; Figure 2—figure supplement1).
evidence: This is a control analysis result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The difference in spatial similarity prior to the SFW cannot be explained by differences in lexical processing of the word before the SFW (SFW-1).
source: The difference in spatial similarity prior to the SFW cannot be explained by differences in lexical processing of the word before the SFW (SFW-1): this word always differed within sentence pairs, and any differences in its lexical properties (visual complexity, word frequency and syntactic class) between members of a pair were matched between pairs that constrained for the same SFW (within-pairs) and pairs that constrained for a different SFW (between-pairs).
evidence: This is an argument based on the experimental design and stimulus properties.

claim: The spatial similarity effect cannot be explained by differences in the predictability of the SFW-1.
source: The spatial similarity effect also cannot be explained by differences in the predictability of the SFW-1: the cloze probability of these words was fairly low (11% on average) and any difference in cloze probability between members of a pair was matched between pairs that constrained for the same SFW (within-pairs) and pairs that constrained for a different SFW (between-pairs).
evidence: This is an argument based on the experimental design and stimulus properties.

claim: In a control analysis with sentences containing the same SFW-1 but predicting different SFWs, the averaged spatial similarity remained larger for the within-pair sentences than the between-pair sentences (t(25) = 1.81, p = 0.08).
source: We found no evidence for this. Instead, we found that the averaged spatial similarity across the −880 – −485 ms interval before the onset of the SFW (corresponding to 120–515 ms after the onset of SFW-1) remained larger for the within-pair sentences (R = 0.072 + /- 0.02) than the between-pair sentences (R = 0.063 + /- 0.03): t(25) = 1.81, p = 0.08 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), although in this subset analysis, the difference only approached significance due to the limited statistical power (on average there were only 40 within-pairs and 29 between-pairs after artifact rejection).
evidence: This is a control analysis result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Previously encountering a sentence ending with the expected SFW did not inflate the spatial similarity between sentence pairs that predicted the same SFW.
source: A repeated measures ANOVA with the factors Order (Expected SFW first, Unexpected SFW first) and Pairs (Within-pair, Between-pair) showed no main effect of Order (F(1,25) = 0.747, p = 0.396, η2 = 0.029), nor an interaction between Order and Pairs (F(1,25) = 1.804, p = 0.191, η2 = 0.067). We conclude that previously encountering a sentence ending with the expected SFW did not inflate the spatial similarity between sentence pairs that predicted the same SFW.
evidence: This is a control analysis result addressing a potential confound.

claim: The spatial similarity associated with pairs that predicted the same specific words was significantly larger than the spatial similarity associated with pairs that predicted the same syntactic category (t(25) = −3.559, p = 0.002).
source: We found that the spatial similarity associated with pairs that predicted the same specific words (within-pair spatial similarity: R = 0.074 + /- 0.02) was significantly larger than the spatial similarity associated with pairs that predicted the same category (within-category spatial similarity: R = 0.068 + /- 0.02), (t(25) = −3.559, p = 0.002; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a control analysis result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The greater within-pair versus between-pair spatial similarity effect was not simply reducible to the prediction of general syntactic category.
source: This suggests that the greater within-pair versus between-pair spatial similarity effect was not simply reducible to the prediction of general syntactic category.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control analysis comparing within-pair and within-category spatial similarity.

claim: The absence of an effect off the diagonal in the cross-temporal spatial similarity matrix suggests that the spatial patterns associated with prediction changed over time.
source: Moreover, the absence of an effect off the diagonal suggests that the spatial patterns associated with prediction changed over time.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-temporal spatial similarity analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The temporal pattern of neural activity was more similar in pairs that predicted the same versus different words over central and posterior sensors (cluster-based randomization test: p = 0.002).
source: When comparing the within- and between-pair temporal similarity topographic maps (Figure 3A), the temporal pattern of neural activity was more similar in pairs that predicted the same versus different words over central and posterior sensors (cluster-based randomization test: p = 0.002; Figure 3A: right panel).
evidence: This is a key result from the temporal RSA analysis at the sensor level, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The temporal pattern of neural activity was more similar in sentence pairs that predicted the same word than pairs that predicted a different word within the left inferior temporal gyrus, extending into the medial temporal lobe including the left fusiform, hippocampus and parahippocampus as well as left cerebellum (p = 0.006).
source: This revealed significantly greater temporal similarity between sentence pairs that predicted the same word (within-pairs) than pairs that predicted a different word (between-pairs) within the left inferior temporal gyrus, extending into the medial temporal lobe including the left fusiform, hippocampus and parahippocampus as well as left cerebellum (p = 0.006; a cluster-randomization approach controlling for multiple comparisons over grid points).
evidence: This is a key result from the temporal RSA analysis in source space, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The spatial pattern of neural activity was more similar in sentence pairs that predicted the same SFW (within-pairs) than in pairs that predicted a different SFW (between-pairs), beginning at around 120 ms after the onset of the word before the SFW.
source: We found that the spatial pattern of neural activity (across sensors) was more similar in sentence pairs that predicted the same SFW (within-pairs) than in pairs that predicted a different SFW (between-pairs). This spatial similarity effect began at around 120 ms after the onset of the word before the SFW (i.e. the SFW-1).
evidence: This is a summary of the main spatial RSA finding.

claim: The spatial similarity effect reflects the greater spatial similarity in the pattern of brain activity produced by the prediction of the same word than the prediction of a different word.
source: We interpret this finding as reflecting the greater spatial similarity in the pattern of brain activity produced by the prediction of the same word than the prediction of a different word.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their main finding.

claim: The spatial similarity effect only became apparent after the onset of the word immediately preceding the SFW (i.e. after the SFW-1), suggesting it is unlikely to have reflected any general differences in the full contexts.
source: The fact that the spatial similarity effect only became apparent after the onset of the word immediately preceding the SFW (i.e. after the SFW-1) suggests that it is unlikely to have reflected any general differences in these contexts (the full set of words prior to the SFW).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of the observed effect.

claim: The observed spatial similarity effect reflects the prediction of the SFW rather than lexical processing of the SFW-1.
source: This strongly suggests that the observed effect reflects the prediction of the SFW rather than lexical processing of the SFW-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control analysis with matched SFW-1.

claim: The increased spatial similarity detected in the within-pair sentences reflects activity related to the prediction of a specific SFW.
source: A second set of alternative interpretations might acknowledge that the increase in spatial similarity detected in the within-pair sentences reflects activity related to the prediction of a specific SFW.
evidence: This is the authors' favored interpretation of their findings.

claim: Several previous studies have reported evidence of anticipatory lexico-semantic processing following constraining relative to non-constraining contexts.
source: This is by no means the first study to show evidence of lexico-semantic prediction before the onset of new bottom-up input during sentence processing. Several previous studies have reported evidence of such anticipatory processing following constraining relative to non-constraining contexts (see Kuperberg and Jaeger, 2016a, section 3.1), at least under experimental conditions that encourage the generation of high-certainty lexico-semantic predictions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The present study provides neural evidence that lexico-semantic predictions are item-specific – different predicted words are associated with spatially distinct patterns of neural activity.
source: What distinguishes the present study from this previous work is that it provides neural evidence that these lexico-semantic predictions are item-specific – that is, different predicted words are associated with spatially distinct patterns of neural activity.
evidence: This is the authors' statement of the novel contribution of their study.

claim: Nouns and verbs are known to have distinct neuroanatomical representations.
source: This is because we designed our study such that 50% of the predicted SFWs were nouns and 50% were verbs, allowing us to calculate the within-category spatial similarity between all pairs of sentences that predicted the same syntactic category. We compared these within-category spatial similarity values with the within-pair spatial similarity values, in which the predicted SFWs shared both syntactic category and lexico-semantic features. We found that the within-category spatial similarity values were significantly smaller than the within-pair spatial similarity values (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). These findings suggest that the within-pair spatial similarity effect did not simply reflect the prediction of the broad syntactic category of the SFW.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the context of interpreting the results.

claim: The spatial similarity effect reflected similarities at the level of the semantic properties and features that defined the meanings of the predicted words.
source: Instead, we suggest that the spatial similarity effect reflected similarities at the level of the semantic properties and features that defined the meanings of the predicted words.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: The prediction of the particular set of semantic properties and features corresponding to a word may be reflected by the activation of a particular spatially distributed network.
source: For example, the prediction of the particular set of semantic properties and features corresponding to the word <baby> (e.g. <human>, <small>, <cries>) may have been reflected by the activation of a particular spatially distributed network that differed from the network reflecting the prediction of the particular set of semantic features corresponding to a different predicted word, <roses> (e.g. <plant>, <scalloped petals>, <fragrant smell>).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how semantic features might be represented.

claim: The increased spatial similarity in association with sentence pairs that predicted the same word may have reflected similarities of predictions generated at a lower phonological and/or orthographic level of representation.
source: It is also possible that the increased spatial similarity in association with sentence pairs that predicted the same word reflected similarities of predictions generated at a lower phonological and/or orthographic level of representation.
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation considered by the authors.

claim: The prediction of semantic features may lead to the top-down pre-activation of information at lower phonological and/or orthographic levels of the linguistic hierarchy.
source: On this account, the prediction of semantic features led to the top-down pre-activation of information at these lower levels of the linguistic hierarchy before new bottom-up information became available to these levels (see Kuperberg and Jaeger, 2016a, sections 3 and 5 for discussion).
evidence: This is a theoretical account cited from previous work.

claim: The spatial similarity effect began at 120 ms after the onset of the word before the predicted SFW (i.e. SFW-1), providing evidence that the prediction of the SFW was generated at the first point in time at which participants had sufficient information to unambiguously generate this prediction.
source: As noted above, the spatial similarity effect began at 120 ms after the onset of the word before the predicted SFW (i.e. SFW-1), even though the effect was not driven by the lexical properties or the predictability of the SFW-1 itself. This provides evidence that the prediction of the SFW was generated at the first point in time at which participants had sufficient information to unambiguously generate this prediction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of the effect.

claim: Following highly constraining contexts, comprehenders are able to predict entire events or states, along with their associated semantic features, prior to the appearance of new bottom-up input.
source: This type of account follows from a generative framework of language comprehension in which, following highly constraining contexts, comprehenders are able to predict entire events or states, along with their associated semantic features, prior to the appearance of new bottom-up input (e.g. Kuperberg and Jaeger, 2016a, sections 4 and 5; Kuperberg, 2016b; St. John and McClelland, 1990; Rabovsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework cited from previous work.

claim: The spatial similarity effect primarily reflects similarities at the level of semantic features associated with the predicted word, rather than similarities of the entire predicted events/states.
source: Importantly, however, we conceive of the spatial similarity effect detected here as primarily reflecting similarities at the level of semantic features (e.g. <human>, <small>, <crying>) associated with the predicted word ('baby'), rather than similarities of the entire predicted events/states (e.g. the <baby sleeping in the crib> event versus the <newborn baby in the hospital> event) (see Kuperberg, 2016b).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of what level of representation their effect reflects.

claim: The spatial similarity effect lasted until 515 ms following the onset of the SFW-1 and then dropped off in the second half of the interval before the onset of the SFW.
source: Despite its early onset, the spatial similarity effect was fairly short-lived: it lasted until 515 ms following the onset of the SFW-1 (corresponding to 315 ms following its offset at 200 ms), and then dropped off in the second half of the interval before the onset of the SFW (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of the spatial similarity effect shown in Figure 2B.

claim: It is possible that the predicted information was not maintained over the relatively long interstimulus interval used in the present study (SOA: 1000 ms per word).
source: It is possible that, the predicted information was not maintained over the relatively long interstimulus interval used in the present study (SOA: 1000 ms per word).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why the effect was transient.

claim: Representations within working memory can be maintained in a silent neural state, instead of being accompanied by persistent delayed activity.
source: This idea has been recently discussed in relation to the notion of 'activity-silent' working memory, which holds that representations within working memory can be maintained in a silent neural state, instead of being accompanied by persistent delayed activity (Stokes, 2015b; Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical concept cited from previous work.

claim: The unique spatial pattern of brain activity associated with the prediction of specific words changed over time.
source: This suggests that the unique spatial pattern of brain activity associated with the prediction of specific words changed over time.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-temporal spatial similarity analysis.

claim: Different semantic features associated with the prediction of a specific word might have been recruited at different time points.
source: We speculate that this may be because different properties associated with particular words became available at different times. For example, the different semantic features (e.g. <human>, <small>, <cries>) associated with the prediction of a specific word (e.g. 'baby') might have been recruited at different time points.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the dynamic spatial patterns.

claim: The prediction of specific words was associated with unique temporal patterns of neural activity.
source: In addition to being associated with unique spatial patterns of neural activity, we also found evidence that the prediction of specific words was associated with unique temporal patterns of neural activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the temporal RSA findings.

claim: A recent study applying temporal RSA to intracranial EEG signals reported that the temporal pattern of neural activity within the left inferior temporal lobe encoded item-specific representations during picture naming.
source: This observation is in line with a recent study that applied temporal RSA to intracranial EEG signals, and reported that the temporal pattern of neural activity within the left inferior temporal lobe encoded item-specific representations during picture naming (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Temporal similarity patterns corresponding to unique lexico-semantic items can be detected before new bottom-up input becomes available.
source: The current findings extend these previous results by suggesting that temporal similarity patterns corresponding to unique lexico-semantic items can be detected before new bottom-up input becomes available.
evidence: This is the authors' statement of how their findings extend previous work.

claim: Damasio (1989) proposed that multimodal semantic features become bound together through a process of 'temporal synchrony' within 'convergence zones'.
source: However, we suggest that it is consistent with a classic theory by Damasio (1989), who proposed that multimodal semantic features, represented in widely distributed regions of the cortex, become bound together through a process of 'temporal synchrony', and that this binding occurs within 'convergence zones', which act to unify these features into a discrete whole (Damasio, 1989).
evidence: This is a citation to a classic theoretical proposal.

claim: The unique temporal patterns of neural activity within the left ventral/medial temporal lobe may have played a functional role in binding the unique sets of semantic features represented by the unique spatial patterns of neural activity.
source: In the present study, it is possible that the unique temporal patterns of neural activity within the left ventral/medial temporal lobe played a functional role in binding the unique sets of semantic features that were represented by the unique spatial patterns of neural activity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional role of the temporal patterns.

claim: The unique temporal patterns of neural activity may have played a role in binding semantic information as it became available dynamically over time.
source: Speculatively, these unique temporal patterns of neural activity may have also played a role in binding this information as it became available dynamically over time (as opposed to becoming available all at once).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the temporal binding mechanism.

claim: A particular temporal signature may have functioned to bind the dynamically evolving and spatially distributed pattern of neural activity into a coherent lexico-semantic representation.
source: For example, by tracking (or perhaps even orchestrating) the particular time-course of accessing the distributed brain regions that represent the semantic features of <baby> (e.g. <human>, <small> and <cries>), a particular temporal signature may have functioned to bind the dynamically evolving and spatially distributed pattern of neural activity into a coherent lexico-semantic representation, corresponding to participants' subjective experiences of predicting a specific word.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how temporal binding might work.

claim: The localization of the temporal similarity effect to the left ventral temporal regions is consistent with the well-established role of these regions in lexico-semantic processing.
source: The localization of the temporal similarity effect to the left ventral temporal regions (left inferior temporal lobe and fusiform cortex) is consistent with the well-established role of these regions in lexico-semantic processing (Lüders et al., 1991; Lüders et al., 1986; McCarthy et al., 1995; Mummery et al., 1999; Nobre and McCarthy, 1995; Visser et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The left ventral temporal regions have been proposed to function as 'hubs' that bring together widely distributed semantic features across the cortex.
source: In particular, it is consistent with the proposed role of these regions as 'hubs' that brings together widely distributed semantic features across the cortex (Patterson et al., 2007; Ralph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Semantic hubs may function as a 'dictionary' by mediating between widely distributed conceptual knowledge and specific word forms.
source: Such hubs may function as a 'dictionary' by mediating between widely distributed conceptual knowledge and specific word forms (orthographic and phonological knowledge) (Caramazza, 1996; Damasio et al., 1996) and/or they play a more domain-general role in semantic processing (Nobre et al., 1994; Patterson et al., 2007; Reddy and Kanwisher, 2006; Shimotake et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and empirical work.

claim: The inferior temporal cortex activity extended into the medial temporal lobe (the parahippocampal gyrus and the hippocampus).
source: Notably, the activity within the inferior temporal cortex extended into the medial temporal lobe (the parahippocampal gyrus and the hippocampus).
evidence: This is a result from the source localization analysis.

claim: The hippocampus plays a crucial role in binding representations to generate predictions.
source: While MEG source-modeling results within medial and subcortical regions should be interpreted with caution, the possible involvement of the hippocampus is interesting given other work that has implicated it as playing a crucial role in binding representations to generate predictions.
evidence: This is supported by reference to other work in the field.

claim: The hippocampus in rats represents upcoming spatial representations as the rat is navigating.
source: A large literature from recordings in rats demonstrates that the hippocampus represents upcoming spatial representations as the rat is navigating (Gupta et al., 2012), and we have a good understanding of the physiological mechanisms supporting such predictions (Lisman and Redish, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: There is growing evidence that predictive mechanisms in the hippocampus might generalize to the human hippocampus.
source: There is also growing evidence that these predictive mechanisms might generalize to the human hippocampus (Chen et al., 2011; Davachi and DuBrow, 2015; Harrison et al., 2006; Hindy et al., 2016; Schiffer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: The temporal patterns in higher frequency bands recorded within the hippocampus were similar between a pre-picture interval and the picture itself, suggesting a role in representing pre-activated non-verbal semantic information.
source: Moreover, recently, it was found that the temporal patterns in higher frequency bands recorded within the hippocampus were similar between a pre-picture interval and the picture itself (Jafarpour et al., 2017), suggesting a role in representing pre-activated non-verbal semantic information.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: It is conceivable that the hippocampus plays an analogous role in language prediction.
source: Given these findings, it is conceivable that the hippocampus also plays an analogous role in language prediction.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on previous findings.

claim: Piai et al. (2016) used intracranial recordings in humans to demonstrate predictive effects in the hippocampus in a language task.
source: Indeed, Piai et al. (2016) used intracranial recordings in humans to demonstrate predictive effects in the hippocampus in a language task in which the sentence-final word had to be produced (Piai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The activity also included the left cerebellum.
source: In addition to the medial temporal lobe, the activity also included the left cerebellum.
evidence: This is a result from the source localization analysis.

claim: Previous studies have reported bilateral cerebellum activation (right dominant) during language prediction.
source: However, previous studies have reported bilateral cerebellum activation (right dominant) during language prediction (Bonhage et al., 2015; Lesage et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cerebellum may play a role in generating item-specific predictions in language processing.
source: Our findings seem to suggest that the cerebellum also may play a role in generating item-specific predictions in language processing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cerebellar activation.

claim: This study does not speak to the debate about whether neural evidence of anticipatory processing at the level of specific word-forms can be detected during sentence comprehension under conditions that do not encourage predictive processing.
source: Before concluding, we emphasize that this study does not speak to the debate about whether neural evidence of anticipatory processing, particularly at the level of specific word-forms (rather than semantic features), can be detected during sentence comprehension under conditions that do not encourage predictive processing (DeLong et al., 2005; Nieuwland et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2017); nor does it address the question of whether such predictions are probabilistic in nature.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The study deliberately used highly constraining contexts to encourage participants to generate high certainty specific lexico-semantic predictions.
source: In the present study, we deliberately used highly constraining contexts to encourage participants to generate high certainty specific lexico-semantic predictions, and we used a long interstimulus interval between words to ensure that we would be able to detect any representationally specific neural activity if it was present.
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: When item-specific lexico-semantic predictions are generated, they are associated with unique spatial and temporal patterns of neural activity.
source: We see the unique contribution of our study as providing evidence that, when we know that item-specific lexico-semantic are generated, they are associated with unique spatial and temporal patterns of neural activity.
evidence: This is the authors' statement of their main contribution.

claim: Unique spatial patterns of neural activity became active at around 100 ms after a word was unambiguously predicted and their activation was transient and dynamic.
source: We showed that unique spatial patterns became active at around 100 ms after a word was unambiguously predicted and that their activation was transient and dynamic.
evidence: This is a summary of the spatial RSA findings.

claim: The prediction was accompanied by unique temporal patterns of brain activity that localized to the left inferior and medial temporal lobe.
source: In addition, we show that the prediction was accompanied by unique temporal patterns of brain activity that localized to the left inferior and medial temporal lobe.
evidence: This is a summary of the temporal RSA findings.

claim: A stimulus set of 120 pairs of sentences in Mandarin with highly constraining contexts was developed.
source: We developed a stimulus set of 120 pairs of sentences in Mandarin with highly constraining contexts.
evidence: This describes the stimulus development process.

claim: The two contexts within each pair were distinct from one another and had no content words in common (with the exception of five pairs), but they each strongly predicted the same sentence-final word.
source: The two contexts within each pair were distinct from one another, and they had no content words in common (with the exception of five pairs), but they each strongly predicted the same sentence-final word (SFW).
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties.

claim: In half of the sentences, the expected final word was a noun and in the other half, it was a verb.
source: In half of these sentences, the expected final word was a noun and in the other half, it was a verb.
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties.

claim: A cloze norming study was carried out in 30 participants who did not participate in the subsequent MEG study.
source: To select and characterize this final set of sentences, we began with an initial set of 208 pairs and carried out a cloze norming study in 30 participants (mean age: 23 years; range: 18–28 years old; 15 males), who did not participate in the subsequent MEG study.
evidence: This describes the norming procedure.

claim: In the final set of stimuli, the mean lexico-semantic constraint was 88% (SD: 12).
source: Across all pairs, the mean lexico-semantic constraint was 88% (SD: 12).
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties based on the cloze norming.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences.
source: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Thirty-four students from the Beijing area were initially recruited by advertisement.
source: Thirty-four students from the Beijing area were initially recruited by advertisement.
evidence: This describes the participant recruitment.

claim: The data of eight participants were excluded because of technical problems, leaving a final MEG dataset of 26 participants.
source: The data of eight participants were subsequently excluded because of technical problems, leaving a final MEG dataset of 26 participants (mean age 23 years, range 20–29; 13 males).
evidence: This describes the final participant sample.

claim: MEG data were collected using a CTF Omega System with 275 axial gradiometers at Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences.
source: MEG data was collected using a CTF Omega System with 275 axial gradiometers at Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition equipment and location.

claim: Six sensors were non-functional and were excluded from the recordings.
source: Six sensors (MLF31, MRC41, MRF32, MRF56, MRT16, MRF24) were non-functional and were therefore excluded from the recordings.
evidence: This describes a technical detail of the data acquisition.

claim: The ongoing MEG signals were low-pass filtered at 300 Hz and digitized at 1200 Hz.
source: The ongoing MEG signals were low-pass ﬁltered at 300 Hz and digitized at 1200 Hz.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: On average, 96% ± 3.4% of trials were retained after artifact rejection.
source: On average, 96% ± 3.4% of trials were retained.
evidence: This describes the data quality after preprocessing.
